newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia set for record gold output - report.
newsitem.headline: Australia set for record gold output - report.

text.p: Australia is on track to retain its position as the world's third largest gold producer behind South Africa and the United States, mining a record 304 tonnes in fiscal 1996/97, a government commodities forecasters said.
The 11 percent rise on last year's output reflects rapid development of new mines in Australia, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.

In its December quarterly report, ABARE said Australian commodities export earnings would grow 2.5 percent in 1996/97 to A$58.92 billion (US$46.54 billion), with minerals and energy the strongest sectors and farm produce weaker.
That compares with a forecast three months ago of A$59.72 billion and a June quarter forecast of A$61.08 billion.
ABARE said the value of minerals and energy should rise 4.5 percent in the year to June 30, 1997, reaching a new high of A$36.3 billion.
Strong earnings from crude oil exports were a major factor and earnings from iron ore and liquified natural gas shipments were also forecast to post gains, the bureau said.
The volume of mine production was seen up by 5.4 percent, similar to the increase last fiscal year, it said.

But prices received by Australia's minerals and energy exporters were forecast to fall by 2.4 percent in 1996/97, in part because of an assumed appreciation of the Australian dollar, currently around US$0.79, which would devalue exports.

"While average prices received for Australian minerals and metals exports are forecast to decline by 5.4 percent in 1996/97, average prices received for energy exports are forecast to increase by 2.4 percent," ABARE said.
In contrast, Australia's farm sector was forecast to be weaker, with export earnings around A$22.6 billion in 1996/97, slightly down from last year's level.

Despite an expected bumper wheat crop, the value of wheat exports was expected to fall by around nine percent as world prices fell, ABARE said. Export earnings for beef and sugar were also seen falling in the current fiscal year.
Farm production was forecast to rise by 7.4 percent in 1996/97 after a 15 percent rise in 1995/96 in the aftermath of the previous year's drought.
Wool exports were seen rising in 1996/97, with Chinese demand remaining firm, although production was expected to decline marginally and prices were expected to fall.
